job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at a desk in the Kellan Institute's machine learning lab, where my master's project is a model that spots faulty welds from photos. Around noon I switch to my own laptop and do paid work, building simple websites for small shops, mostly with an AI assistant doing the first draft. I live in a student block on Quarry Street and my dad drives a bus, so there's no money coming from home. I owe about 33,000 and my bank account usually sits near zero by the 20th.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say honestly that I'd be a bit surprised, because I use it all day and it already feels like a real shift. But fine, if it stalls, then it stalls, and the tools I know would still be handy. I'd tell my friends the people selling magic were overselling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change my situation much. I'd still have 33,000 of debt and few openings in town, and AI skills would just be one more line on my application. I'd quietly be relieved that my master's isn't about to lose its meaning, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and push my freelance work harder, maybe six or seven clients instead of three. I'd also apply to about 40 jobs, mostly remote ones, since there are almost no machine learning roles in this town. I'd use that welding project as the main thing I show people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Nothing's on fire, I'm just short of cash all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would it mean if it stopped improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn about 600 a month from freelance sites and clients like Mrs Pitt's bakery. Rent takes 380, food and the bus pass take most of the rest, and my loan repayments don't start until I earn above a line I haven't reached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal month of money look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd just be a normal tool, like spreadsheets. I'd keep using it every day and I'd want to understand the limits better. It doesn't threaten me, but I keep an eye on how fast it's moving.

say: I'd say the people selling **magic** oversold it, but the tools are still handy.
I'd tell friends my **welding project** shows real skills.
think: Privately nothing changes much: **33,000 debt** and few machine learning roles in town.
I'd be quietly relieved my **master's** keeps its meaning.
do: Push **freelance work** from three clients to six or seven by the summer.
Apply to **40 remote jobs** this year, since town has almost no machine learning roles.
feel: **Calm-ish**, just short of cash all the time.
S0.quote: I use it all day and it already feels like a real shift.
fieldNote: Ben treats AI as an everyday **tool** and is comfortable in the flat scenario.
His money gets in the way, not the technology.
Freelance income of about 600 a month is his buffer.

steps.text: Take on six or seven small web clients instead of three
Apply to 40 remote machine learning jobs by spring
Finish the weld-detection master's project and publish the code

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn. I'd tell everyone I know, in plain terms, to get hands-on with these tools instead of arguing about them. But I'd also say we need rules, like a union for people whose work gets automated, and no one wants to hear that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing is, I'm already a junior doing what AI does for people. If a company can get first drafts of code for free, why would it pay a graduate for them? I think the bottom rung is where it bites, and I'm standing on it. I'd be better than most because I'm using the tools, but there are a lot of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start charging for something that isn't just code, like helping small shops work out what to automate. I'd get two or three proper case studies and join a tech workers' union that's forming online. I'd also save 100 a month, because I'd want some buffer before a first full-time offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick at the same time. It's a good ride, but I don't have a seatbelt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an AI that does your job better look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two things. The cheap website jobs go first, because a shop owner can do it herself with a prompt. The bigger ones, where someone has to understand what the shop actually does, stay for a while. So I'd move up the ladder fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your freelance work change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of me, honestly. Other graduates are using the same tools and the same prompts, so everyone's output looks the same. The edge is knowing what to ask and having a person trust you.

say: I'd tell everyone to get **hands-on** with the tools, and push for a union for automated workers.
I'd say rules matter, even if nobody wants to hear it.
think: I'm already a junior doing what **AI does**, so the bottom rung is where it bites.
I'd be better than most, but there are **a lot of me**.
do: Sell **automation advice** to small shops instead of plain websites.
Join the online **tech workers' union** and save 100 a month.
feel: **Excited and sick** at once, a good ride without a seatbelt.
S1.quote: I think the bottom rung is where it bites, and I'm standing on it.
fieldNote: Ben sees the problem clearly because he uses the **tools** himself.
He answers with a move up the value chain and a union.
The seatbelt line hints at how little cushion he has.

steps.text: Offer small shops a paid audit of what they could automate
Join the online tech workers' union and attend the monthly call
Put 100 a month into a separate savings account
Build two case studies using AI agents for local firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing since electricity and we are unprepared. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd demand a basic income and a ban on firms firing people for software without notice. I'd do it online, at rallies, whatever's available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm both in the best and worst place. I know the tools, which helps, but my entire first job is the first thing to go. And the master's will be useless in eighteen months. If everyone can do my work in a prompt, it doesn't matter that I'm good at prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating the master's as the point and start earning. I'd chase every freelance client I could get, take a warehouse or driving job on the side if needed, and put whatever I made into a cheap savings account. I'd join the union and the basic income campaign, and I'd tell my dad to avoid new loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired and frightened, honestly. I'd sleep badly and also feel weirdly alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no safety net ready. Governments don't move in two years, and companies move in two weeks. By the time any support exists I'd have used up my freelance money, so I'd want to move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'no time to prepare' mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move out of the Quarry Street block into a cheaper room, maybe a shared house for 250 a month. And I'd call the university to ask if they'd freeze my course fees. Small steps, but I'd rather do something than refresh the news.

say: I'd say this is **bigger than electricity** and we are unprepared.
I'd demand a **basic income** and notice before firms replace staff with software.
think: My whole **first job** is the first thing to go, and the master's loses its worth.
If everyone can do my work in a prompt, being good at **prompting** doesn't help.
do: Chase every **freelance client** and take a driving or warehouse job on the side.
Move to a **250 a month** shared house to cut rent.
feel: **Wired and frightened**, sleeping badly but oddly alive.
S2.quote: If everyone can do my work in a prompt, it doesn't matter that I'm good at prompting.
fieldNote: Ben's skill gives him **no safety** in this world, and he knows it.
He combines campaigning and a hustle, a typical adaptive reaction.
He worries about his dad's debts, which he does not mention elsewhere.

steps.text: Chase every freelance client and take weekend driving shifts
Move to a 250 a month shared house before the lease renews
Join the basic income campaign and write to local representatives
Attend union meetings and help organise one rally in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, and we'd be foolish to waste it. I'd tell friends to start saving and learning, and I'd tell the government to start the basic income pilots now. Waiting for a crisis is how we get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see it as a window. If I get a decent job right away and I use these years to build real expertise in a field that needs trust, like medical imaging, I'd be fine for a while. I'd still expect the thinking work to go by 2031, so I'd treat each year as a bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job offered, anywhere, and use it to learn how a company runs. I'd save 200 a month and pay down the loan, and keep my freelance as a second leg. I'd move toward a domain like healthcare, where regulation keeps people in the loop for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, actually. Uneasy, but with a plan I can read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably turn the weld model into a real product for a small manufacturer and try to get one paying customer. Even one customer would be proof that someone trusts me with something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your master's project become?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a scramble, five is a plan, ten is nearly a career. I'd pick five if I could, because it makes me work hard but not panic.

say: I'd call five years a **gift** and say governments should start basic income pilots now.
I'd tell friends to start **saving and learning** this year.
think: I could use five years to become an expert in a field that needs **trust**, like medical imaging.
I'd still expect the thinking work to **go by 2031**, so each year is a bonus.
do: Take the **first job offered** and save 200 a month.
Keep **freelance** as a second leg and aim for one paying customer for the weld model.
feel: **Okay**, uneasy but with a plan I can read.
S3.quote: Two years is a scramble, five is a plan, ten is nearly a career. I'd pick five if I could, because it makes me work hard but not panic.
fieldNote: Ben turns time into **sequence**: job, savings, domain expertise.
He expects thinking work to go on schedule and plans accordingly.
Healthcare is his chosen shelter because regulation slows replacement.

steps.text: Accept the first graduate job offered and learn how the firm runs
Put 200 a month into savings and loan repayments
Sell the weld-detection model to one small manufacturer
Take an online course in medical imaging and its regulation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, but only if people use it. I'd push for training funds and a basic income pilot now and tell everyone to learn the tools while they're easy to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good. I'd have a decade to build a career, pay off the loan and maybe start something. I'd expect to change what I do two or three times, but I like that. It sounds like a game with enough lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in a good team and keep my own projects on the side, because I learn faster that way. I'd try to pay off the loan in six or seven years and put aside a bit toward a flat. I'd also do a night course in something people-heavy, maybe management or teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed. Alive, even. There's enough time to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad not to worry, that I'd be okay and I'd take him on a holiday. He drives a bus, so he's worried about his job too, and I'd want him to hear it from me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell him the bus driving part will likely last longer than my work will. That's a funny thing to say, but it's true.

I'd push for **training funds** and a basic income pilot now.
think: I'd feel pretty good, with a decade to **build a career** and pay off the loan.
I expect to change what I do **two or three times**, and I like that.

feel: **Relaxed**, almost alive, with enough time to enjoy it.
S4.quote: I'd expect to change what I do two or three times, but I like that. It sounds like a game with enough lives.
fieldNote: With ten years Ben is almost **cheerful**; the debt is the only thing keeping him uneasy.

steps.text: Join a good machine learning team and keep side projects going
Pay off the loan within six or seven years

Tell my dad the plan and help him with his own worries

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I know the tools, and it would still wipe out the job I'm training for, before I've paid anything off. What would help is a basic income, retraining that's actually free, and rules that give workers notice before a firm swaps them for software. And a cheap place to live.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only this. Everyone assumes I must be fine because I use AI every day, but using it every day just means I can see it more clearly.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes I must be fine because I use AI every day, but using it every day just means I can see it more clearly.
portrait: Ben is 24, doing a **machine learning master's**, with 33,000 of debt, almost no savings and a bus-driver father with nothing spare.
He builds websites for small shops with AI help, earning about 600 a month, and uses these tools **all day**.
He is progressive: he wants unions, a basic income and rules, and blames big tech and slow governments.
His moods run from uneasy to anxious, since using AI daily lets him see his own entry job vanish.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which wipes out his training before he has paid anything off.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **basic income**, free retraining, notice before firms swap staff for software, and cheap housing.
